questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly defines a stateful firewall, as Lesson 1 presents it?
options: Tracks the state of every active connection in a state table, and automatically permits reply traffic matching an already-established connection
Evaluates every packet independently against a static rule set, with no memory of prior traffic
Inspects packet payload content to identify the specific application generating traffic
Runs as an agent on an endpoint, watching local file and process activity
Sits inline and can actively drop or reset a matching connection in real time
Requires a separate inbound rule to be written for every expected reply packet
questions.explain: Lesson 1 defines a stateful firewall by its state table: it tracks which connections an internal host actually opened, and when a reply comes back matching one of those entries, it passes the reply automatically with no separate inbound rule needed. That's the behavioral shift from reasoning about individual packets to reasoning about connections.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes a stateless firewall, not a stateful one — Lesson 1 explicitly contrasts the two, and it's the stateless firewall that keeps no memory of past traffic and forces an administrator to write an explicit rule for every expected reply, which is the opposite of what a stateful firewall's state table already handles automatically.

questions.prompt: Two employees both generate HTTPS traffic on port 443 — one browsing a legitimate business application, one browsing a blocked social media site. Per Lesson 2, what specific capability lets an NGFW tell the two apart when a traditional stateful firewall can't?
options: Deep packet inspection combined with application awareness, since the NGFW can identify the specific application generating the traffic rather than just the port it travels on
The firewall's state table, since it already tracks which connections were initiated internally
802.1Q VLAN tagging, since it labels which VLAN the traffic originated from
Placing one of the two services in a DMZ, since public-facing servers are isolated there
questions.explain: Lesson 2 explains that a traditional stateful firewall only sees connection-level facts — both connections here look identical at port 443 over HTTPS. An NGFW's deep packet inspection examines the payload itself, and application awareness lets it identify the specific application generating the traffic, so a rule can target 'Facebook' or 'social media' directly instead of blocking port 443 and breaking every HTTPS service.

questions.prompt: Match each DMZ-related term from Lesson 3 to what it actually means.
right: A server, like a web or mail server, that must be reachable from the internet
Two separate firewalls with the DMZ sandwiched between them, requiring two independent hops to reach internal
A network segment between the internet and internal network used to host public-facing servers
One firewall with three interfaces enforcing separate rule sets for internet, DMZ, and internal zones
questions.explain: A DMZ is the buffer segment itself; a three-legged DMZ builds it with one firewall holding three interfaces, each with its own rule set; a back-to-back DMZ uses two independent firewalls with the DMZ between them for extra defense in depth; and a public-facing server is the kind of host — a web or mail server — the DMZ exists to host in the first place, per Lesson 3.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 4, the standard that tags Ethernet frames with VLAN membership so a single trunk link can carry traffic for multiple VLANs at once is called ________ tagging.
questions.explain: 802.1Q tagging inserts a small tag into each Ethernet frame identifying its VLAN membership before it crosses a trunk link, so the receiving switch can read that tag and deliver the frame only to ports on the matching VLAN, even though multiple VLANs' traffic physically shares the same cable, exactly as Lesson 4 describes.

questions.prompt: A SOC analyst just read about a new attack pattern in a threat report and wants to add a detection rule for it. Per Lesson 5, why would they typically deploy that rule in IDS mode before ever enabling it in IPS mode?
options: Because an IDS only alerts and can never cause a real outage if the new rule misfires on legitimate traffic, letting the team tune it against real traffic and confirm a low false-positive rate before trusting it to block
Because IDS mode is a mandatory prerequisite before any rule is technically permitted to run in IPS mode on the same sensor
Because IPS mode can only run vendor-supplied signatures, never a custom rule a SOC writes itself
Because Snort and Suricata are structurally incapable of running the same rule set in both IDS and IPS mode
questions.explain: Lesson 5 explains the real tradeoff: an IPS sits inline, so a false positive on a brand-new, untuned rule becomes a real outage — it blocks legitimate traffic outright. An IDS never touches the live packet, so running the rule there first lets a team confirm it's reliable with zero risk of breaking anything, before ever flipping it to blocking mode.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about signature-based and anomaly-based detection, per Lesson 6.
options: Signature-based detection matches traffic against a database of known attack patterns and generally has a low false-positive rate when it fires
Anomaly-based detection can catch a genuinely novel attack that has no published signature yet
Anomaly-based detection has a lower false-positive rate than signature-based detection
A brand-new attack technique with no published signature sails through a purely signature-based engine completely undetected
Most modern detection platforms, including Suricata, run both engines side by side rather than picking just one
questions.explain: Lesson 6 is explicit that signature-based detection is precise with few false alarms but blind to anything with no documented signature yet, while anomaly-based detection catches novel attacks precisely because it isn't tied to a known pattern — at the cost of a higher false-positive rate, not a lower one. That's exactly why platforms like Suricata run both engines together rather than choosing one.

questions.code: alert tcp any any -> $HOME_NET 80 (msg:"Possible SQL Injection Attempt"; content:"UNION SELECT"; sid:1000001; rev:1;)
questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 7, every custom Snort/Suricata rule must include a unique numeric ________ field, like the 1000001 shown in the rule above, so an analyst or another tool can reference that exact rule unambiguously.
questions.explain: Lesson 7 identifies `sid` as the rule option that gives every rule a unique numeric ID, with locally written rules conventionally starting at 1000000 and up specifically to avoid colliding with the official rule sets' IDs — exactly the field shown as `sid:1000001` in this example.

questions.prompt: An attacker who already has a foothold on one internal server escalates privileges and modifies a system file to maintain persistence, generating no unusual network traffic at all. Per Lesson 8, why would a NIDS watching the wire miss this attack completely while a HIDS on that same host catches it?
options: Because the activity never crosses the network, and a NIDS can only see traffic that crosses the wire, while a HIDS watches that host's own file integrity and process activity directly, from the inside
Because NIDS tools like Snort and Suricata are structurally incapable of detecting privilege escalation under any circumstances, even over the network
Because a HIDS has visibility into every host on the network segment, while a NIDS only ever watches the one host it's installed on
Because file integrity monitoring is a NIDS capability rather than a HIDS capability
questions.explain: Lesson 8 draws this exact distinction: a NIDS's visibility is limited to what crosses the network, so a local privilege escalation and an in-place file modification are both structurally invisible to it. A HIDS agent like OSSEC watches the host's own logs, file integrity, and process activity from the inside, which is precisely the blind spot a NIDS cannot cover.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 9, a NetFlow flow record is built around the ________ — source IP, destination IP, source port, destination port, and protocol.
questions.explain: Lesson 9 names the 5-tuple as the core of a flow record: source IP, destination IP, source port, destination port, and protocol, plus the facts a device can observe without opening the payload, like packet count, byte count, and duration.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes NetFlow flow data from Deep Packet Inspection (DPI), as Lesson 10 presents them?
options: Flow data records metadata like source/destination and byte counts without examining payload content, while DPI examines the actual payload to identify what the traffic really is
Flow data examines packet payload content in detail, while DPI only ever records connection metadata
Flow data and DPI are two different names for the exact same inspection technique
DPI is cheap enough to run continuously on every link across a large network, while flow data is too resource-intensive to run broadly
Flow data requires buffering and reassembling application-layer data, while DPI only ever reads header fields in passing
DPI has fully replaced flow monitoring because it is strictly better in every respect
questions.explain: Lesson 10 draws a clean line: flow data (Lesson 9) only ever says who talked to whom, how much, and for how long, without opening the payload. DPI opens the payload itself to say what the application actually did — an HTTP POST, a database query, a malware signature inside the content — which is exactly the depth flow metadata deliberately leaves out.
questions.distractorExplain: Option D reverses the real cost tradeoff from Lesson 10. Flow data is the cheap, always-on option precisely because it only records header-level metadata; DPI is the resource-intensive one, since it has to buffer and reassemble payload content, which is exactly why DPI runs at specific chokepoints like a perimeter firewall rather than across every link in the network the way flow collection can.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about traffic baselining, per Lesson 11.
options: A traffic baseline is a profile across multiple dimensions — volume, destinations, and timing — not a single number
A single, network-wide average baseline would catch the same anomalies a per-host baseline catches
A backup server legitimately transferring tens of gigabytes to a storage array at 2 AM can be completely normal for that specific server
Baselining has to be scoped per host or per segment type, because a single network-wide average would blur legitimate differences together
Baselines are built from full packet capture data rather than from flow data
questions.explain: Lesson 11 is explicit that a baseline is a profile across volume, destinations, and timing, built from flow data over days or weeks, scoped per host or segment type precisely because a network-wide average would blur a backup server's legitimate 2 AM transfer together with a workstation doing the same thing, which would actually be a red flag for that host.

questions.prompt: Match each exfiltration-related term from Lesson 12 to what it actually describes.
right: Unauthorized transfer of data out of a network to an external destination
A destination registered only a few weeks ago — a detail threat intelligence feeds commonly flag as suspicious
Encoding stolen data inside the subdomain portion of DNS queries to evade normal filtering
Regular, periodic check-ins from compromised traffic to a command-and-control server at a fixed interval
questions.explain: DNS tunneling hides stolen data in DNS query subdomains because outbound DNS is almost always allowed; beaconing is the regular check-in rhythm that gives malware away even when the destination alone looks unremarkable; a newly registered domain is a supporting signal threat intel flags; and data exfiltration is the overall unauthorized transfer these techniques carry out, exactly as Lesson 12 lays out.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about EDR telemetry categories, per Lesson 13.
options: Process creation telemetry captures a process's full command-line arguments, not just the fact that it started
Registry telemetry matters for catching persistence mechanisms, such as a new value written to a Run key
File-based signature scanning alone is sufficient to catch process injection, since the injected code is written to disk as a new file
Network connection telemetry is tagged to the specific process that opened the connection
DLL/module load telemetry can catch an attack even when no new file was ever written to disk
questions.explain: Lesson 13 draws the key distinction between 'a process ran' and 'here is its exact command line' as the foundation of process creation telemetry, and explains that registry telemetry catches persistence via Run keys while network telemetry is tagged by initiating process. Process injection specifically has no new file on disk at all — it's memory-resident code loaded into an already-trusted process — which is exactly why DLL/module load telemetry, not file scanning, is the signal that can catch it.

questions.prompt: Lesson 14's concrete example walks through a process tree built from a phishing attachment. Put these processes in the order they actually launched, from the root to the final hop.
questions.explain: Per Lesson 14, a user opens an invoice attachment in Outlook, which opens the document in Word — unremarkable on its own. Word then spawns PowerShell, the classic red flag since a document editor has no legitimate reason to launch a scripting engine, and PowerShell in turn spawns certutil, a built-in Windows utility often abused to download or decode payloads. Each additional hop down that chain adds confidence it's a staged attack rather than a one-off coincidence.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 15, a legitimate, pre-installed system tool like certutil, WMI, or PsExec that an attacker repurposes for malicious action instead of bringing in custom malware is called a ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 15 names LOLBins as legitimate, often signed system tools repurposed for malicious use. The attack isn't in the tool itself — it's in how it's used, which is exactly why signature-based antivirus has nothing new to flag when an attacker runs certutil or PsExec, tools already trusted and already present before the attack began.

questions.prompt: A compromised host is running a fileless, memory-resident attack. Per Lesson 16, why does isolating the host from the network preserve more forensic evidence than powering it off?
options: Running processes, injected code, active connection state, and encryption keys in use all live in volatile memory (RAM), which a power-off destroys instantly, while isolation keeps the machine running and reachable while cutting off its network access
Powering off a machine automatically generates a complete memory dump before the shutdown finishes
Isolation and powering off destroy exactly the same evidence, so there is no meaningful difference between the two responses
A fileless attack writes all of its evidence to disk by definition, so powering off the machine has no effect on what can later be recovered
questions.explain: Lesson 16 explains that isolation cuts off a host's network traffic while leaving it running, so an analyst can still pull a full memory dump and build an accurate forensic timeline. A fileless attack, by definition, never wrote most of what matters to disk, so powering off destroys the only copy of evidence that ever existed — exactly the loss isolation is built to prevent.

questions.prompt: Match each IOC type from Lesson 17 to its example.
right: A repeated phishing subject line hitting dozens of inboxes in the same hour
A fixed-length fingerprint that still matches a known-malicious file even after it's renamed and moved to a new folder
A documented piece of attacker infrastructure, such as a command-and-control server, that can be blocked at the firewall
A new entry added under a Windows Run key so a program launches automatically at startup
questions.explain: Lesson 17 covers all four IOC types: a cryptographic hash matches on content alone, so renaming or moving the file never breaks the match; a malicious IP/domain is documented attacker infrastructure, like the WannaCry kill-switch domain; a registry key artifact is a classic persistence mechanism under a Run key; and an email-based IOC is a recurring phishing pattern a SOC recognizes before anyone opens an attachment.

questions.prompt: A Threat Intelligence Platform (TIP) automatically pushes a newly reported malicious IP to the firewall's blocklist within minutes of a feed update. Per Lesson 18, why does that automatic loop matter more than a SOC simply reviewing the feed manually once a day?
options: It lets the SOC defend against infrastructure before it ever reaches the organization, instead of leaving a window of exposure open until the next manual review
It replaces the need for a SIEM to ever enrich an alert with feed context again
It guarantees that specific IP address will never be reused by any other threat actor in the future
It eliminates the need to subscribe to commercial vendor feeds, ISACs, or open-source feeds going forward
questions.explain: Lesson 18 makes the point directly: the value of a feed isn't the list itself, it's that the list updates before an attacker's infrastructure even reaches the organization. A TIP automating that feed-in, block-out loop closes the exposure window to minutes, where a once-a-day manual review would leave that same IP unblocked for up to a full day.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 19, ________ is the HTTPS-based transport protocol that defines how STIX threat-intel content actually moves from a server to a subscribing organization's client.
questions.explain: Lesson 19 pairs STIX (the data format) with TAXII (Trusted Automated eXchange of Indicator Information), the HTTPS-based API specification that defines how a TAXII client pulls or subscribes to STIX bundles hosted in collections on a TAXII server.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about OSINT for defenders, per Lesson 20.
options: Shodan is a search engine that indexes internet-connected devices and exposed services, which a defender can use to search their own public IP ranges
WHOIS records show who registered a domain, when, and through what registrar
OSINT requires hacking into systems or stealing data to gather useful information
A breach database like Have I Been Pwned can show whether an employee's work credentials have appeared in a leaked dump
The tools defenders use for OSINT are entirely different from the tools attackers use during Reconnaissance
questions.explain: Lesson 20 defines OSINT as gathering from sources that are already publicly available — nothing hacked or stolen — and names Shodan, WHOIS, and breach databases as the defender's core toolkit. It also makes the point that these are the exact same tools an attacker uses during Reconnaissance; what differs is only who's looking and why, not the tools themselves.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes what a vulnerability scanner like Nessus or OpenVAS actually does, per Lesson 21?
options: It probes a target and checks it against a database of known vulnerabilities, missing patches, and misconfigurations — it finds problems but does not fix them
It discovers brand-new, never-seen-before vulnerabilities that no plugin or NVT has ever documented
It automatically installs the needed patch or changes the configuration once it finds an issue
It can only be run against a target that is already confirmed to be compromised
Nessus and OpenVAS are two different names for exactly the same proprietary product
It replaces the need for a CVE catalog or a CVSS severity rating entirely
questions.explain: Lesson 21 is explicit that a scanner systematically checks a target against vulnerabilities it already knows about — its plugin database (Nessus) or NVT library (OpenVAS) — and that scanning is strictly a detection activity: it reports a finding tied to a CVE, but remediation is a separate step carried out afterward by an administrator.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B is backwards from what Lesson 21 explains. A scanner only checks a target against vulnerabilities already cataloged in its plugin or NVT database; it does not discover brand-new, undocumented flaws on its own, which is exactly why a scan reporting zero findings doesn't prove a host has no vulnerabilities at all — it only proves none of the known checks matched.

questions.prompt: An authenticated scan of a Windows server, logging in with a domain account, finds an outdated local PDF reader and a registry setting that weakens a security control — neither of which an unauthenticated scan of the same server ever reported. Per Lesson 22, why couldn't the unauthenticated scan see either one?
options: An unauthenticated scan interacts purely over the network with no credentials, so it can't log in to enumerate installed software or inspect local configuration and registry values
Unauthenticated scans are not capable of identifying open ports or reading service banners at all
The authenticated scan was run against a different plugin/NVT database than the unauthenticated scan
Unauthenticated scans only work against Linux hosts, never against Windows servers
questions.explain: Lesson 22 explains that an unauthenticated scan mirrors an outside attacker's view: no credentials, so no ability to log in and look around. Only an authenticated scan, logging in with valid credentials, can enumerate installed software and exact versions and inspect registry values directly, which is exactly how it found the outdated PDF reader and the weakened registry setting the unauthenticated scan structurally could not see.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about prioritizing vulnerability scan findings, per Lesson 23.
options: A Medium-severity finding on an internet-facing server with a publicly circulating exploit can reasonably be treated as more urgent than a Critical-severity finding on an isolated lab machine
Real prioritization weighs severity, exploitability, and asset criticality together, not just the raw CVSS score
Sorting strictly by raw CVSS score, highest first, is exactly how a working analyst should prioritize remediation
Asset criticality considers how important and how exposed a specific host is, independent of the vulnerability's raw severity
A scan report's remediation guidance field gives the specific fix, such as a named patch or a configuration change
questions.explain: Lesson 23's own worked example is a Medium-severity finding on an exposed, actively-exploited server reasonably outranking a Critical finding on an isolated lab machine, precisely because severity alone is 'the same number no matter where the vulnerable system sits.' Real prioritization weighs severity, exploitability, and asset criticality together — sorting by raw CVSS alone is exactly the shortcut Lesson 23 warns against.

questions.prompt: Put these core steps of the vulnerability management lifecycle, per Lesson 24, in the correct order.
questions.explain: Lesson 24 walks through the cycle in this exact order: scan the target systems, prioritize findings by severity, exploitability, and asset criticality, remediate by applying the fix, and verify by rescanning to confirm the fix actually worked — before the whole cycle repeats, because new vulnerabilities are disclosed constantly.

questions.prompt: A decoy file server named FINANCE-BACKUP-2024 has no real data and no legitimate application configured to connect to it. Per Lesson 25, why does a single login attempt against it carry far more confidence as a sign of attack than a single login attempt against a real production server?
options: Because no real user or process should ever interact with the honeypot, so any interaction with it is inherently suspicious, with no legitimate baseline to rule out first
Because the honeypot runs more sophisticated detection software than a typical production server does
Because production servers never log any login attempts at all, legitimate or otherwise
Because a dedicated team reviews only honeypot alerts, while production server alerts go completely unreviewed
questions.explain: Lesson 25's core logic is that a honeypot serves no legitimate business purpose whatsoever, so there's no 'normal' baseline to establish and no legitimate traffic to filter out first. A production server's single login is ambiguous — backup job, user, or attacker — while the honeypot's entire normal state is silence, so any interaction with it is already evidence.

questions.prompt: Match each honeypot concept from Lesson 26 to what it actually is.
right: The containment a high-interaction honeypot requires so an attacker's real access can't reach anything else
A real, fully-functional system an attacker can actually log into and explore — high realism, higher operational risk
Simulates a service minimally, such as a fake SSH banner, with no real system behind it — low risk, low realism
A scripted stand-in for a real service, used to look real without actually being real
questions.explain: Lesson 26 contrasts a low-interaction honeypot's thin, scripted simulation — safe but limited to the shallowest layer of an attack — against a high-interaction honeypot's real, fully-functional system, which produces far richer intelligence but requires rigorous isolation and segmentation precisely because an attacker can genuinely interact with it.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 27, a fake credential, file, or database entry planted so that any access to or use of it triggers an alert — without standing up a dedicated decoy system — is called a ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 27 introduces the honeytoken as a single piece of bait, like a fake AWS access key or a fake 'VIP customer' database record, sitting inside a real environment. It works on the same underlying principle as a honeypot — nothing legitimate should ever reach for it — but at far lower cost, since it can be dropped almost anywhere in seconds with no infrastructure required.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of Lesson 29's Castellan Retail segmentation design in the order the lab actually builds them.
items: Stand up a single perimeter firewall with WAN, DMZ, and Internal interfaces
Move the public order-tracking web server into the DMZ, alone with its reverse proxy
Write the WAN-to-DMZ rule allowing only tcp/80 and tcp/443 to the web server
Split the internal network into VLANs 10 (Workstations), 20 (Servers), and 30 (Guest Wi-Fi)
Scope the DMZ-to-internal rule to one host and one port rather than subnet to subnet
questions.explain: Lesson 29 builds the design in exactly this sequence: the three-legged firewall comes first as the foundation, then the web server moves into the DMZ alone, then the narrow WAN-to-DMZ allow rule, then the internal VLANs split by role, and finally the DMZ-to-internal rule scoped to one host and one port — the step the lesson calls out as the one most flat-network designs get wrong by opening broad subnet-to-subnet access instead.

questions.prompt: Lesson 30's beacon-detection rule above matches on `dsize:<100` and a `threshold` of 20 hits in 300 seconds, with no malware-specific content string. Why does that make it more durable against an attacker who switches to a new C2 tool next month than Rule 1's exact `sqlmap` User-Agent match?
options: It detects the behavioral shape of beaconing — small, regularly recurring requests — rather than one specific tool's identifying string, so a different C2 tool producing the same small-and-regular pattern still trips it
Because `dsize` and `threshold` simply make the rule execute faster than a content match, which is the only reason it matters
Because threshold-based rules can only ever be written for HTTP traffic, unlike content matches
Because the rule specifically blocks sqlmap regardless of which User-Agent string that tool happens to send
questions.explain: Lesson 30 draws exactly this contrast: Rule 1 matches an exact string (`sqlmap` in the User-Agent), so it breaks the moment an attacker's tool changes. Rule 2 matches on size and frequency — the shape of beaconing itself — so a brand-new C2 tool that still checks in with small, regular requests gets caught by the same rule, with nothing tool-specific to go stale.

questions.prompt: In Lesson 31's slow-exfiltration case study, select every true statement about the three signals that together confirmed the compromise.
options: The NetFlow baseline deviation flagged a brand-new destination contacted on a suspiciously regular interval, not any single large transfer
The threat-intel-flagged destination alone was already enough to confirm malicious activity, with no other signal needed
EDR process telemetry showed the outbound connections coming from a disguised executable running out of a user-writable temp folder, not from an approved application
Each of the three signals came from a different chapter's tools, and none of them alone was sufficient to be conclusive
The response used EDR isolation and a perimeter block specifically to avoid disturbing the evidence still running in memory
questions.explain: Lesson 31 is explicit that no single signal was enough: the flow deviation alone could have been a new SaaS tool, the flagged IP alone could have been a stale intel entry, and the disguised process alone might have sat in a lower-priority queue. Together — baseline deviation, threat intel, and EDR telemetry from three different chapters — they were conclusive, and the response isolated the host via EDR rather than powering it off, preserving the memory-resident evidence.
